content: The guidelines recommend implementing intensified adherence interventions to reduce HIV-related morbidity and mortality. Rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) within seven days of an HIV diagnosis is advised for individuals living with HIV, following confirmation of diagnosis and clinical assessment. Same-day ART initiation is also recommended if the individual is willing and ready to start treatment immediately, unless there are clinical reasons to delay. The 2017 WHO consolidated guidelines on person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance emphasize the use of unique identifiers to link individuals across health services. Routine data collection is recommended for care and reporting on programmatic, national, and global HIV indicators, including key global targets. The 2016 WHO guidelines on integrating collaborative tuberculosis (TB) and HIV services for people who inject drugs provide updated recommendations on managing TB, HIV-associated TB, HIV, viral hepatitis B and C, drug dependence, alcohol dependence, malnutrition, mental illness, and psychosocial needs. These guidelines build on the 2008 WHO policy for collaborative TB and HIV services. The 2017 WHO guidelines on the public health response to pretreatment HIV drug resistance address resistance to non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors in individuals with no prior ART exposure or those reinitiating first-line ART. This document supplements the 2016 consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for HIV treatment and prevention. The 2017 WHO consolidated guideline on sexual and reproductive health and rights of women living with HIV outlines strategies to create enabling environments and provide health interventions for these women. It addresses gender equality, human rights, and adolescent-specific recommendations, such as counseling adolescents on the risks and benefits of disclosing their HIV status and initiating ART for all adolescents living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count. The 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations focus on men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons, sex workers, and transgender people. These guidelines introduce a comprehensive package of interventions, including health-sector actions, service delivery, and monitoring processes. The 2017 WHO clinical guidelines for responding to children and adolescents who have been sexually abused provide trauma-informed care recommendations. They include post-rape care, psychological support, and ethical considerations for mandatory reporting. For HIV, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is recommended for children and adolescents who have been raped, with a 28-day prescription of antiretroviral medicines following risk assessment. Adolescents at high risk of HIV should have access to comprehensive prevention methods, including pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), voluntary medical male circumcision, and ART to reduce viral load and prevent transmission. Structural drivers of HIV, such as social and gender norms, must also be addressed. Adolescents require accessible HIV testing services, including self-testing, without mandatory parental consent. Community-based distribution of self-test kits has shown high uptake among adolescents. Barriers to accessing HIV prevention and care services include stigma, inconvenient service hours, and prohibitive costs. Peer-based interventions, community-based services, and support groups can enhance linkage to care. Policies on age of consent for HIV testing and treatment should protect adolescents' rights to make health decisions. Adolescents transitioning between pediatric, adolescent, and adult care face challenges due to inadequate health worker training and poor service linkages. Effective planning and support are needed to ensure smooth transitions. Frequent viral load monitoring is recommended for adolescents at high risk of antiretroviral resistance. Adolescents living with HIV should receive counseling on contraception and prevention of mother-to-child transmission, as they are more likely to experience unintended pregnancies and detectable viral loads during pregnancy. Disclosure of HIV status requires sensitive, non-judgmental support, with individualized planning on how, when, and to whom to disclose. Community-based adherence support programs, such as those implemented by Kheth’Impilo in South Africa and AfricAid in Zimbabwe, have demonstrated improved retention and viral suppression among adolescents. These programs use trained community health workers and adolescent treatment supporters to provide adherence counseling, psychosocial support, and structured group interventions. The Zimbabwean Zvandiri model, recognized as a best-practice intervention, integrates community-based services with clinical care provided by government and private clinics.
